theme: 饮食-古籍中的静心茶饮

content.text: Jingyan, after our tea gathering, I sketched this quick drawing. The tea tasted quite light, but its aftertaste lingered, much like the value of ‘slowness’ we discussed earlier.

Yu An, your painting reminds me of the courtyard after a tea gathering, where guests have departed and the courtyard is quiet, yet the warmth lingers in the cup. This subtle yet profound experience is precisely the art of dining and drinking that the ancients sought to pursue.

Yes, while drinking, my attention unconsciously drifted to my breath and the birdsong outside the window. The flavor is indeed very subtle, but after taking a sip, there's a lingering sweetness in the mouth, and I feel completely calm.

This reminds me of the 'focused perception' you mentioned earlier. The tea itself is simple, but the process of brewing and savoring it is like 'conversing with the paper' when restoring ancient texts—it requires complete immersion.

Yes! It reminds me of some clients who struggle with traditional meditation due to high anxiety. Perhaps starting with "mindfully eating a piece of fruit" or drinking a cup of tea could serve as an entry point to mindfulness.

The ancients said that the 'art of dining' was inherently connected to self-cultivation, but modern people often separate the two, pursuing a fast-paced approach to eating. This aligns closely with the 'value of slowness' we are discussing.
Jingyan, you're right. I'm thinking perhaps I could occasionally incorporate such simple 'mindful eating/drinking' sessions into my art therapy workshops, as a warm-up or transition.

This is a great idea. Just like in this photo, the steady hand and calm mind while serving tea are a form of practice in themselves. But remember the reminder from our collaboration on the 'Little Guide to Mindfulness': avoid dogma and stay open.

I understand, just like your mindset of 'following the material' when restoring ancient texts. I will design it to guide participants to observe the color, texture, and taste of the food, rather than forcing a specific outcome.

Well, this can help the client establish a 'gentle barrier,' much like what you've learned from the experience of excessive empathy. The lightness of the tea might just symbolize this attitude of non-attachment.

Yes, and it reminds me of the memorial album we made for Mohen, which carried that sense of 'cherishing without attachment.' Mindful eating can also become a daily form of remembrance, treasuring the present moment.

Yu An, your associations are always so sharp. It's like the focus of a craftsman tuning an instrument in a documentary, or the 'uselessness that is useful' when I restore Buddhist scriptures—seemingly simple, yet deeply meaningful.

Thank you. I plan to try it out in next week's workshop, starting with a cup of tea to guide everyone to slow down. This will also continue our theme of "The Value of Slowness," offering a way to resist the fast-paced rhythm.

That sounds very meaningful. If you need, I can share more ancient tea recipes from old texts, but the key still lies in the state of mind during brewing, just as emphasized in 'Ancient Tea Invitation'.
That's great! We can incorporate this into the 'Mindfulness Guide' collaboration project as a new chapter. However, I'll first practice it myself to ensure it flows naturally and doesn't seem abrupt.

Okay, I support you. Just like creating a commemorative album, from concept to specifics, this tea gathering experience has already inspired new possibilities. I'm really looking forward to seeing how it develops.
Jingyan, this tea gathering has truly been a great learning experience for me. From your calm guidance to our current mutual enrichment, I feel our collaboration is deepening more and more.

Yuan, I have also learned a great deal from your creativity and inclusiveness. Our conversations over tea are not just about food and drink, but also about how we can integrate mindfulness into our lives to achieve harmony between ourselves and the world around us.
Well, I'll keep exploring and share the progress. Just like the journey from emotional exhaustion to mindful recovery, every step is worth taking slowly.
Stillness cultivates wisdom, slowness is speed. Stay in touch, wishing you peace and a pleasant tea gathering.
